market_context: United States; vegetable calcium content and bioavailability.
title: Vegetables Highest in Calcium

seo.title: Vegetables Highest in Calcium per 100 Grams
seo.meta_description: Collard greens, kale, bok choy, and watercress can provide meaningful calcium. Absorption matters: spinach calcium is poorly absorbed because of oxalate.
seo.search_intent: Compare calcium-rich vegetables while accounting for both content and bioavailability.

excerpt: Some leafy greens contain substantial calcium: raw collards and certain kale entries can exceed 200 mg per 100 g, bok choy is around 100 mg, and broccoli around 45–50 mg. The number alone is not enough, because spinach calcium is much less bioavailable due to oxalate.
content_html:
A table of calcium milligrams can be misleading if it stops at total content. Spinach contains roughly 100 mg calcium per 100 g, yet only a small fraction is absorbed; low-oxalate vegetables such as kale, bok choy, and broccoli can contain less total calcium while delivering more absorbable calcium.

How much calcium do common vegetables contain?

Raw vegetableApprox. calcium/100 g
Collard greens~230 mg
Kale, depending on type~150–250 mg
Watercress~120 mg
Bok choy~100 mg
Spinach~100 mg
Broccoli~47 mg

These values rank total calcium, not the amount your body will absorb. Cultivar, maturity, and whether the vegetable is raw or cooked also shift the exact number.

Spinach shows why “more calcium” can mean less usable calcium

The NIH estimates calcium absorption from spinach at only about 5%, compared with roughly 27–30% from milk. Spinach is high in oxalate, which binds calcium and sharply limits availability.

Human studies of low-oxalate greens show a very different pattern: fractional absorption has been measured at roughly 49% from kale, 54% from bok choy, and over 60% from broccoli in the tested portions. Those percentages are not a fixed guarantee for every meal, but they show why total milligrams alone can give the wrong ranking.

A serving-size example makes the difference concrete

In one published comparison using servings around half a cup, 85 g of bok choy supplied about 79 mg calcium and an estimated 42.5 mg absorbable calcium. A similar 85 g serving of spinach contained about 115 mg total calcium but only about 5.9 mg was estimated to be absorbed. Spinach contained more calcium on paper, while bok choy delivered several times more usable calcium in that example.

Cooking changes the numbers without destroying calcium

Heat does not destroy a mineral such as calcium. What changes is water and food weight: leafy greens collapse during cooking, so 100 g cooked can represent far more plant material than 100 g raw. Boiling can also move some minerals into the cooking water if that liquid is discarded.

Do vegetables have to provide all of your calcium?

No. Vegetables can contribute meaningfully, but total intake also depends on portion size and the rest of the diet. Dairy, fortified plant beverages, calcium-set tofu, canned fish with bones, and other foods may contribute depending on what you eat.

For plant calcium, combine total content, serving size, and bioavailability. Kale, bok choy, and broccoli are especially useful because their calcium is absorbed far more efficiently than calcium from spinach.

faq.question: Which vegetables are highest in calcium?
faq.answer: Collard greens and some types of kale are among the highest common vegetables, often above 150–200 mg per 100 g.

faq.question: Is spinach a good calcium source?
faq.answer: It contains calcium, but high oxalate makes much of it poorly absorbed.

faq.question: Does broccoli have much calcium?
faq.answer: It has less total calcium than many leafy greens, around 45–50 mg per 100 g, but the calcium is relatively bioavailable.
